body_markdown:
Speed is weird. On the one hand, it is a question of physics, simply calculated by dividing distance covered by the time required to go that distance. There are more variables in real life, though, which complicates the matter. Not to mention that our perception of speed gets muddied by the physiological limitations of our bodies, which at times struggle to make sense of what the f@&# is going on when the sensation of high speed gets intense. I came to this dual understanding recently, while negotiating the dry, sandy channel of a broad wash in western Arizona, as I piloted the raucous rolling laboratory of a Ford Bronco Raptor.


The truck’s various powertrain and chassis computers were busy with the calculations, the big numbers of the Bronco’s digital speedometer climbing, climbing, climbing as I stood on the throttle. Some combination of the human vestibular system, motion parallax, and a good old-fashioned butt dyno were clocking my experience, no doubt broadcasting their findings across my wide-eyed face. Result: a big, dumb grin.


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


The pale colors of smoke trees and catclaw and sand—so much sand—passed outside my windows in a smear. I finally looked down to see the speedo registering 70, which, I should add, feels nothing like 70 you cruise at on a freeway. If anything, that speed on loose, bumpy terrain is more akin to plowing over rough waves in a boat. Every signal in your body screams that you’re going 170. Fast enough, I decided; time to conclude this thrilling little experiment.


I wasn’t alone in ripping across the desert. Mine was but one of around 500 Raptors—not just new Broncos—that had converged on Arizona’s Lake Havasu City for Raptor Rally 003. It’s an annual gathering of Ford’s rowdy off-roaders, two days of dusty mayhem and camaraderie. The weekend started at a much slower, far more deliberate pace, however.


## Raptor Off-Roadeo


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


When Ford launched the Bronco and Bronco Sport back in 2021, it also established a handful of[Bronco “Off-Roadeo”](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/new-half-day-program-opens-bronco-off-roadeo-to-the-public/) events: driving programs across the country offering half-day and full-day instruction to owners looking to get the most out of their new Broncos when off the beaten path. One of those spots, tucked into the desert terrain east of Las Vegas, was recently rebranded as the Raptor Off-Roadeo, and will now be an instructive playground for anyone who owns or has an interest in the Bronco Raptor, Ranger Raptor, or the one that started it all back in 2010, the F-150 Raptor.


Ford assembled a coterie of media to serve as the fortunate guinea pigs for the program, including yours truly, and upon arrival, we were each assigned a Bronco Raptor for the weekend. My steed: a 6500-mile Oxford White hoss.


We have spilled plenty of ink on this site about[Raptors generally](https://www.hagerty.com/media/great-reads/jurassic-park-driving-every-raptor-to-celebrate-15-years-of-madness/) and[Bronco Raptors specifically](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/33-critical-questions-with-the-2023-ford-bronco-raptor/) , but the refresher course is as follows: 418 broncopower and 440 lb-ft from Ford’s twin-turbocharged V-6; advanced 4WD with seven selectable modes, including the venerable “Baja”; electronic front and rear lockers, with stabilizer-bar disconnect; 37-inch BFG KO2 tires; 13 and 14 inches of suspension travel, front and rear; 13.1 inches of ground clearance; and 37-inch water fording capability. The Bronco Raptor will hit 60 mph in 5.6 seconds, putting it on par with another famous twin-turbo, the Z32 Nissan 300ZX, which could not, for the record, ford a river.


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


We did not attempt to do so, either, thankfully, because when water flows in these parts it does so violently. So much so that any passage is hugely risky to life and air intake. But I did slow-roll the network of rocky two-track trails out to “Raptor Valley,” where instructors had set up a high-speed Baja-style course for us to sample. On the way there, the facility’s lead trail guide, Anthony Csuzi, gave frequent instruction over the radio—the sorts of tips he’s been doling out for a few years now and what prospective participants can expect to hear.


Three big ones stand out:


“ **Give a little left-foot brake** through washboards, just dragging it about 1%, to shift the balance from the back tires to the front, which allows all four corners to get to work with the suspension.”


“ **Scan forward** and drawn down your line of sight. On every straight, look at the next turn, then incrementally take in what’s coming up ahead. A boulder? A tree?”


“Just like our BFG tires, **Brake before turns, not mid-corner** . That’s when bad things happen to good people. **Flow through the turn** ; let it pull you around like a slot car. **Gas exiting the turn** , as you’re spinning the wheel back to straight.”


Ford understands the crazy capabilities of its trucks, of course, and instructors like Csuzi see real value in making sure owners do, too. “We not only want to give them a great day—we want to educate them on how to be a proper off-road driver.”


Csuzi grew up off-roading and pre-running in the desert and always heard about crashes. “It happens every weekend. There’s always a horror story. So we’re here to impart some safety—how to read the terrain, how to use the equipment when you need it, when to engage lockers or disconnect the stabilizer bar, when to just abandon the line and rethink it before you commit to something bad. It’s so common to just mob through stuff or over-commit, but we’re in the business of keeping these trucks, and their drivers, stable and upright.”


Ford


Out in the old quarry now serving as Raptor Valley, we put some of those pointers into practice and got some speed beneath us. Not absurd, maybe 35 mph, over the short, tight course that included a few step-downs, a tightly banked turn, some short straights, and, finally, a small jump.


I didn’t have a chance to scout the jump ahead of time, I didn’t see anyone else go over it, and I’d never left *terra firma* in car before, so I wasn’t sure what to expect. In retrospect, I’m also not too sure what happened. I wasn’t going all that fast. I *think* I got some air, but with all that travel in the suspension, the Bronco simply could have stuck its big ol’ tires down, like giant training wheels, to remain in contact with the ground the entire time.


What’s that age-old question again? *If a Bronco Raptor jumps in the desert and you’re not around to see it take off, does it get air?*


I needed more clarity on the Bronco’s capabilities here, and I planned to get it the following day, at Raptor Rally 003.


## Raptor Rally


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


Raptor Rally began three years ago, first in northern Utah, as a way for Ford to bring together owners of F-150 Raptors, Ranger Raptors, and Bronco Raptors for some grungy playtime in their highly capable off-roaders. About 300 trucks showed up, and after that first year, the event moved to Lake Havasu City to better take advantage of the suitably vast Bureau of Land Management acreage that surrounds the place. Last year attracted about 400 trucks to a site called Standard Wash, and this year, nearly 500 came out, with around 1100 registered participants and tickets ranging from $150 to $1000.


There is little prestige to the affair. No gleaming 18th fairways here, no VOSS water. Instead, “Basecamp” is set up in a huge, flat, dusty lot beside a sandpit and quarry operation. Inside the gates are vendors, food trucks, club booths, workshops, Ford Performance displays, an R/C track, a stage, and as much shaded seating as possible. Mid-October temperatures still creep into the 90s here, and the sun doesn’t exactly get dim on a cloudless day just because it’s fall.


The parking lot, as expected, was a veritable Raptor sanctuary, with plenty of Arizona, Nevada, and California plates, but also Texas, Colorado, Nebraska, and states farther afield. Utah Raptor Runs, that state’s official club, organized a drive down that included an 80-mile stretch from St. George to Las Vegas—entirely off-road. One owner drove his truck to the event *from New Hampshire* .

Very few people stuck around at Basecamp. Beyond some well-attended Q&A with Ford off-road racing pros, most Rally attendees spent their time exactly where Ford hoped they would: in their Raptors.


The rally featured four designated routes to explore, and they offered enough technical sections and wide-open stretches to fully test the capabilities of man and machine alike. It was out there that I put Csuzi’s principles to work, particularly the “scan forward” bit. Best not to beach this bad boy on a boulder, eh?


A $500 general admission pass included entry for two plus parking for the visiting Raptor and a chance to… jump said Raptor. Folks who purchased the top-tier VIP passes also gained entry to hot-lap ridealongs with pro drivers in a 720-hp supercharged Raptor R and Ford’s Dakar-crushing Raptor T1+, as well as a jump attempt, guided Sunset Trail Drive, and dinner up in the hills above the city.


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


Sunset in the desert is spectacular and everything (really, it was), but we all came for the adrenaline rush of mashed gas pedals and dancing suspension. And air time. I really needed that clarity! After watching trucks in earlier time slots get their air, with photographers standing by to document it, I had high hopes.


And I wasn’t disappointed. Helmet on, I got my instructions in the staging area: Set the bright orange G.O.A.T dial (Goes Over Any Terrain) to the aforementioned “Baja” mode, the 4WD-high setting for high-speed loose-terrain that makes the throttle response aggressive, the steering tight, the Fox dampers agile, and the exhaust rowdy.


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


“You wanna hit the first little baby jump at 38 mph, then aim for 46 mph on the second,” said the Ford Racing tech. “Full throttle to the cones and then completely off throttle in the air.”


“No gas in the air,” I repeated. Having already spent some time watching truck after truck successfully stick the landing here, I had complete confidence in my Bronco and almost that much in myself. “No gas in the air,” I said one more time, for good measure. No need to add four rapidly rotating tires to the mix, no need to introduce a lot of unwanted force to them upon landing.


“Go for it!” the tech shouted, so I did. It doesn’t take long for the truck’s turbos to spool, but even before they did, the rear end sat back on its long-travel suspension as the big Dana axles doled out the power. Baja mode’s lazy traction control sort of reined it in, and by the time I’d hit 25 mph or so, things felt mostly settled, nothing fighting against me or itself to keep in a straight line over the washboards. I’d hit 35 by the time I got to the cones for the first jump. Off the gas and over I went. It felt… exactly like the jump from the day before—almost not there and so easily gathered in by the Bronco. I mashed the throttle again and this time benefitted from the turbos’ anti-lag system, borrowed from the Ford GT, which keeps them spooled and ready for action. Power delivery was immediate, and I actually had to back off early before arriving at the cones for the second jump.


Yeeeehaaaaa!


Dusty Wooddell


Queue the famous scene from *Ferris Bueller’s Day Off* , the one with the parking lot attendants soaring over you in slow motion to the *Star Wars* theme. That is how this one felt—a foreverness to the sensation—at least until touchdown, which was far more jarring than I’d anticipated.


Not nearly so jarring, however, as my experience out at the sandpit a bit later in the day, when the hot laps began. There I found Ford Racing driver Loren Healy ready to chauffeur me around in the Raptor R. His[Instagram bio](https://www.instagram.com/loren_healy/?hl=en) lists him as “Professional Off-Road Racer and Fun-Haver,” and the 3400 posts that follow seem to back up both claims. He’s a multiple King of the Hammers winner, Pikes Peak class winner, Baja champ, and much more, and he was clearly in Fun-Haver Mode once we were buckled into the R. The truck is pretty much exactly as he and Vaughn Gittin Jr. race it in the stock class in Baja, minus the safety equipment. All of which made for a thrilling, violent rollercoaster of a ride up, down, and through the soft gravel and rocks inside the pit. It was all over so quickly and, keen for more of it, Healy shouted, “Wanna go again?” I mean, if I *have* to…


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


Out in the sandpit, Healy was keen to chase down Ford’s Raptor T1+ Dakar entry, which was being driven by Mitch Guthrie.


Years ago, when SCCA Pro Rally came to my town, I snagged a hot lap with Andrew Comrie-Picard in his Mitsubishi Evo. At some point during the ride, which felt like it was on the verge of being out of control, he said to me over the radio, “This is probably five or six-tenths.” When Healy and I concluded our second lap in the Raptor R, he said to me over the radio, “That was 90-to-100 percent. I can push this thing a lot harder than the race truck, because I need to keep that one running for a thousand miles.”


Few people understand the limits of these trucks better than Healy. He has been racing off-road for 20 years and got involved in the Ford sphere when it re-released the Bronco in 2021. He took part in durability testing, and he and Gittin helped develop the Off-Roadeo experience for new Bronco owners.


“So many people buy Raptors and don’t even know how to put them in four-wheel drive,” Healy said. “So the vision of Off-Roadeo, and now Raptor Roadeo, is to be able to understand those people, because ultimately, we want to be able to inspire them. Whether the vehicle is part of the adventure or just there to get them to the adventure—camping or hiking or whatever—we want them to have the confidence to take these trucks off road, because stuff like that changes you for the better.”


Beyond educating people how to drive their trucks on dirt, rocks, and sand, Healy also spoke about stewardship—not of the trucks, but of the land he and Ford are encouraging so many owners to go out and explore. “We get to teach them the ethics, to stay on the trail, to pick up your trash. All the stuff that is so important, because we’ve got to keep these areas open. This is what we love to do, and if we don’t take care of it, we’ll lose it.”


## Winding Down at Basecamp


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


Back at Basecamp, I walked the parking lot checking out row after row of Raptors, noting plenty with aftermarket touches—auxiliary lighting, bed-mounted single and dual spares, overlanding accessories, through-the-bed long-travel suspensions. I also spotted a couple hi-po Hennessey VelociRaptors. Even stock, though, as Healy had deftly illustrated, these trucks are so unbelievably capable—far more competent at what they do than nearly anything else you can drive off a dealer lot. Ford seems eager for others to challenge the Raptors in showrooms, so they can keep raising the bar.


In my wandering, I encountered a couple beside their Bronco. Gabriel and Heidi had driven down from the Bay Area to attend this, their third Raptor Rally. They first got a taste of off-roading when Heidi bought a Toyota 4Runner TRD Pro, then Gabriel quickly realized what he really wanted was a Bronco Raptor. He said the community that has emerged behind the Raptor brand over the last 15 years plays a big part in their enjoyment, and Ford has fostered it well.


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


“The first time I went out I happened to meet a bunch of guys in a Bronco group, and I go out with them all the time now. That’s what’s so much fun about this,” Gabriel said. “The community is great. And Ford does the best events. We jumped! We took a ride in the R!” Then, after a quick glance at his Ruby Red Metallic Bronco, he added, “It’s the best thing we ever did.”


Late in the day, when the place was nearly empty, I took stock of all the club tents, 10 in all. I wanted to check in on Daniel Martin, from Nevada Raptor Runs. We’d met the previous afternoon in Vegas and talked Raptors for a few minutes, and something he said resonated with me; it also spoke to the passion that drives these owners.


He’s on his second F-150 Raptor now. “But the truck I had before that was an F-150 that I built into a Raptor,” he said. “It had a full Raptor body and bed, and it was wide like a Raptor, with Raptor suspension front and back. Just missing some technology that Raptors have, but if you looked at it, you couldn’t even tell that it used to be a regular F-150. That’s how much I love these trucks.”


I get it. From my brief stint behind the wheel of the Oxford White Bronco Raptor loaner, ambling along at Off-Roadeo, hooning at high speed through the open desert, and catching air at Raptor Rally, it was obvious why anyone who experiences one of these things can’t go back to a garden-variety Explorer. Raptors are aspirational and relatively attainable at the same time. Sure, you could get one and never do anything but go mall-crawling with it. But Ford can’t wait to show you what a shame that’d be. Instead, might I suggest finding a long, dry channel somewhere, scanning the line before you, and then covering a great distance in a short time.


Do not attempt.


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)
